tldr: With AI agents speeding up change in brownfield microservices, pull requests must carry evidence of consequences, go to qualified reviewers, and map to EU rules (AI Act, GDPR, CRA, NIS2, DORA).
summary: Breña, who works at the London trading company IG, focuses on how senior engineers work with AI agents in brownfield systems, not on models. The problem: people rotate, knowledge lives in heads, and a small agent-assisted change that passes review can still break production by touching a Kafka contract or a database schema. With fragmented context and several teams moving faster in different parts of the system, he argues, agents speed up the spread of these failures. A green pipeline plus a cosmetic review is not enough. Breña wants stronger ownership, communication, specification and validation.

A good pull request should document its consequences: that consumers don't break, that it complies with regulation, and how to roll it back, which is not always possible. Reviewers should be chosen by the kind of change and must have the authority to stop and revert it. He then walks through the regulations. Depending on a system's classification, the EU AI Act requires human oversight and stored evidence. GDPR covers data minimisation, logging and propagating deletions downstream. The CRA covers secrets, insecure defaults, the SBOM and deserialization. NIS2 covers incident reporting, third-party SDKs, privileged access and untested recovery. DORA covers resilience, concentration on a few providers, recovery plans and inventory.

His practical suggestions: label pull requests produced by AI agents, add pipeline gates that collect regulation-related evidence, check that rollback really works, and watch database migrations, which agents still handle poorly. He also recommends contract tests for REST and messaging, the parallel change pattern for schema evolution, monorepos so an agent sees a whole subsystem rather than one service, shared team skills for common stacks, and spec-driven development to pin down requirements. The talk is short (about 19 minutes) and mostly slides with checklists, with no live demo.
keyPoints: A small agent-generated change can pass a green pipeline and still break production by altering a Kafka contract or database schema used by other services.
PRs should include evidence of consequences: consumers not broken, regulatory fit, and a tested rollback path.
Reviewers should be selected by change type and have the authority to stop and roll back. Not everyone should approve everything.
The EU AI Act requires human oversight for some system classifications, so changes must be classified and evidence stored.

Breña's per-regulation checks for a repository: GDPR (data minimisation, propagating deletions), CRA (secrets, insecure defaults, SBOM, deserialization), NIS2 (incident reporting, third-party SDKs, privileged access, untested recovery) and DORA (resilience, provider concentration, recovery plans, inventory).
Agents still handle database migrations poorly; parallel change (expand/contract) avoids breaking changes on large production databases.
Monorepos give agents the context of a whole subsystem, unlike the one-service-one-repo microservice layout.
takeaways: Label pull requests generated by AI agents in your pipeline.
Add a PR section on consequences: affected consumers, data and regulatory impact, rollback plan.
Verify that your pipelines can actually roll back, including database migrations, and keep evidence that they can.
Use the parallel change pattern for schema changes and contract tests for REST and messaging interfaces.
Consider grouping a subsystem's services in a monorepo so agents get the full context.

quotes.text: A small pull request review will only be considered as a cosmetic review. And this is the starting point.

watchIf: You ship AI-assisted changes to regulated microservices in the EU and want a checklist that ties PR review to the AI Act, GDPR, CRA, NIS2 and DORA.
